en: [ACT III]
(Same set.)
[SCENE I]
CLAUDE, FRANCIS : (Francis is seated at the table and writing a prescription.)
FRANCIS : In short, it is nervous exhaustion, and a tonic will do you good.
CLAUDE : You will be able to reassure Mother; besides, I don't understand why anyone should get so worked up over so little.

FRANCIS : Deep down, it's on account of the illness our father died of, you understand; but there is no connection whatever. (He rises.) There. So, twice a day, a tablespoonful before the main meals; and now, my dear fellow, I must run along as fast as I can.

CLAUDE : Listen, I would like to take advantage of our being alone. But you must promise to tell me the truth. Won't you? I'm counting on it... It's this: it's about what happened years ago at Saint-Loup.
FRANCIS : I suspected there was something preying on your mind.
CLAUDE : It's about me. I would like to know whether you, for instance—did you approve of me when I forgave her? Did you?...

FRANCIS : You surely understand that I never presumed to have an opinion on that. In such cases, everyone acts according to the dictates of his heart or his conscience, or whatever you will. I even confess that the meaning of your question escapes me.
CLAUDE : Were you... surprised?
FRANCIS : Why no, not at all... Given your character, your beliefs, heavens, even your...
CLAUDE, in an ambiguous tone : "My profession?..."
FRANCIS : Insofar as it corresponds to your personality, yes, no doubt...
CLAUDE : You found it completely natural.
FRANCIS : But really, what are you getting at, my dear fellow?
CLAUDE : That was simply what I wanted to know.
FRANCIS : I still believe today that what you did then was in keeping with the course of your life. (A silence.)
CLAUDE : Thank you, you have answered me very clearly.
FRANCIS, taking his head in his hands : What does all this mean? Could it be that?... Oh! Never mind my patient, he will wait, I want to get to the bottom of this.
CLAUDE : It is of no interest, I assure you.
FRANCIS : You are sliding into neurasthenia... Ah, I was terribly wrong not to send that Michel Sandier packing, because after all there is no doubt...
CLAUDE : If that ambiguity existed in my life, it was better that it be dispelled.
FRANCIS : What ambiguity?
CLAUDE : But don't you understand! One has lived for years on a certain idea of oneself, one believed one drew strength from that idea, and one realizes that one was perhaps shamefully mistaken.
FRANCIS : Who is talking about that?

CLAUDE : Perhaps. One isn't even sure... So one no longer knows, one is lost... After all, my thoughts, my words from back then, all of that ought to be transparent to me, I ought to know my way around them as in my own house... Well, no, it is impenetrable to me.
FRANCIS : Right now, you seem to me to be splitting hairs. Only, be careful: those little, very Protestant games are not without danger.
CLAUDE : Those dangers, I do not fear them. Every day I see people who look upon me as their conscience.
FRANCIS : So much the worse for them.
CLAUDE : If I don't even have the courage to read within myself...
FRANCIS : It is not a question of courage. (He has risen.) Come, I really must leave you. But watch out; one pays for that sort of nonsense, and sometimes very dearly.
CLAUDE : Francis, speak to me as a man, not as a specialist.
[SCENE II]
THE SAME, EDMÉE
EDMÉE : Why, I didn't know you were here.
FRANCIS : Mother asked me to drop by; Claude's appearance had worried her, and you know how easily she takes fright.
EDMÉE : And so?
FRANCIS : It's nothing, a touch of nervous fatigue. But the blood pressure is normal, and there's nothing wrong with his heart. (In an undertone.) Well, has your boarder arrived?
EDMÉE : Yes, yes, he is trying to find room for his tub in his bedroom.
FRANCIS : Ah! Ah!
EDMÉE : Yes, that is his great preoccupation at the moment.
FRANCIS : Goodbye, old fellow... so I'm counting on it, right! Goodbye, Edmée. (He exits.)
[SCENE III]
EDMÉE : So you are feeling unwell?
CLAUDE : Not at all. Once again, it was Mother who got it into her head...
EDMÉE, looking at him : You look unwell.
CLAUDE : Leave it be.
EDMÉE : Ah! It's my fault. If you only knew how much I blame myself...
CLAUDE : You revealed your innermost thoughts to me; I have no right to reproach you for that.
EDMÉE : My innermost thoughts! But do I even know them?...
CLAUDE : Then, the day before yesterday?...
EDMÉE : Oh yes, I was sincere; only I don't know, nothing holds, nothing is solid. Where there was a floor, there is an abyss.
CLAUDE : That's it exactly, an abyss.
EDMÉE : But even that abyss, it closes up.
CLAUDE : Meaning that one turns away from it.

EDMÉE : I assure you, the discovery that seemed so profound, that hurt enough to make you scream, becomes nothing; you wonder how you ever believed in it. You see, I have thought about it a great deal since the other day. When those sorts of flashes suddenly flare up, you only have to close your eyes. You have to give yourself credit.
CLAUDE : Fine, delude yourself willfully, feed on illusions; I cannot.

EDMÉE, quivering : Until now, have I been the one who deserved that reproach? Tell me. (A silence; firmly:) You have no right to doubt yourself; you are there to give us strength. It's your calling, after all... I cannot bear your giving up. Just think of what I am going through right now... that man... if I cannot find support in you...

CLAUDE, deeply : I had believed that forgiveness (a movement from Edmée) was an act of charity, the act of a Christian. If I merely fled from scandal or loneliness... And now that you have forced me to open my eyes, you come and clap both your hands over them so that it will be dark again. But what do you want of me? What have I done to you?
EDMÉE : I am weak. You must help me.
CLAUDE : Not at any price. Not at the price of a lie. I cannot. I will not. (A long silence.)
EDMÉE, in a changed tone : Very well. Deep down you are right. We must look things in the face.
CLAUDE : There is no other way.
EDMÉE : Only, don't you think many questions will confront us? To begin with, we are no longer the only ones involved.
CLAUDE : Is it Osmonde you are speaking of?
EDMÉE : Not only of Osmonde... That man who is going to die, to what did we sacrifice him?
CLAUDE : Enough.

EDMÉE : I'll answer in your place: to our selfishness, to our cowardice. (One feels she is on the verge of tears; she has turned away from Claude, her shoulders shaken by a shiver.) So that is the balance sheet; I spare myself no more than I spare you.
CLAUDE, in a sort of start : All the same, I saved both of you.
EDMÉE : From what?
CLAUDE : Without me, what would have become of you? He would have deceived you in your turn.
EDMÉE : Granted: what was the price of a fidelity like yours?
CLAUDE : He would have made you suffer.
EDMÉE : You know, when goodness is nothing but a professional virtue...
CLAUDE : And the little one... if she had a home...
EDMÉE : What a heartwarming home!... Oh, I understand you, believe me, in the face of this bankruptcy...
CLAUDE : There is no bankruptcy; whatever my weaknesses may have been, I am what I believed myself to be. It is useless for you to try to destroy me...
EDMÉE : There might perhaps be a way to prove it.
CLAUDE : What?
EDMÉE : That you truly are the man you believed yourself to be.
CLAUDE : Why is there so much cruelty in your eyes? What have I done to you?
EDMÉE : You have done nothing to me... You were you, I was me, we married each other, that is enough. And as for what you call my cruelty, you know, twenty years of suffering...
CLAUDE : Suffering?
EDMÉE : I no longer even knew how much I suffered, I had forgotten it. I only knew it in the very beginning, long before meeting Michel, when I understood that deep down, for you, love...
CLAUDE : I loved you even in that way.

EDMÉE : No, there was an intact force in you; you spent it on me as with a girl of the streets, but that wasn't love, you know that very well. And the rest, your love for my soul... The woman in me, you didn't satisfy her, you didn't even suspect her.
CLAUDE : The woman in you?
EDMÉE : Yes, you cannot understand. Oh! It's probably not your fault. All of that is the ransom for your virtues. (A silence.)
[SCENE IV]
THE SAME, FRED
FRED, pushing the door slightly ajar : Excuse me...
EDMÉE : What is it? In future, it will be better to knock, you see.
FRED : It definitely won't fit in. (An inquiring glance from Claude to his wife.)
EDMÉE : The tub?

FRED : I don't know what ought to be done, I've come to ask your advice. I had eight francs in excess baggage charges because of it, so it's rather a nuisance; perhaps it could be sold? (To Claude.) Monsieur, I would also like to ask your advice. Is it really worth attending Bergson's lectures? Some people say they're wonderful... So, since Papa writes telling me to make the most of my stay... Only, what embarrasses me is that right at that very time there's a fencing class at the fencing master's, right next door; and since Mama urges me not to neglect physical exercise... Monsieur, what do you think?... Are they really as wonderful as all that?
EDMÉE : Bergson or fencing?
FRED : Bergson, Madame; fencing, I know what that is...
EDMÉE : It is difficult to answer you now; we are busy at the moment; in a little while, if you don't mind?
FRED : I beg your pardon. (He exits.)
[SCENE V]
EDMÉE : And in three years, that boy will be in charge of souls in some little corner of the Jura.
CLAUDE, in a strangled voice : What did you mean just now? What is this proof?
EDMÉE : You really insist on knowing?
CLAUDE : What is it?
EDMÉE : Well then! I saw him again.
CLAUDE : You went to his place?
EDMÉE : We had an appointment at the Lutetia, that's where he lives; we went out together; but he can hardly walk, he gets tired immediately; we sat down on a bench.
CLAUDE : And then?

EDMÉE : He didn't reproach me at all anymore, and that was even worse than the other day. He talked to me about his illness. And above all, he questioned me about Osmonde. He is asking when he will be able to see her again.
CLAUDE, forcefully : I do not want him to see her again.
EDMÉE, in an ambiguous tone : Very good.
CLAUDE : First of all, under what pretext? Already the girl was intrigued the other evening; we would have to tell her everything. It's impossible. She could never bear it.
EDMÉE, as above : You think she is so fragile?
CLAUDE : After all, you yourself, Edmée, can you bear the thought that your daughter... would sit in judgment on you?
EDMÉE : So it's on my account? No, please, I am not taken in by this charade.
CLAUDE : I see what you are thinking.
EDMÉE : That's possible.
CLAUDE : But it's false; it is not out of cowardice, it is because I refuse to shatter her pointlessly.
EDMÉE : That is the crux of it.
CLAUDE : Pointlessly, I repeat: she can do nothing, no one can do anything for him. He is doomed. He is a doomed man.
EDMÉE : I don't know why you are shouting like this. I had asked you to answer yes or no... I merely note that the day a real sacrifice was asked of you...
CLAUDE : That is false.
EDMÉE : I said a real sacrifice.
CLAUDE : It is not because it's a sacrifice.
EDMÉE : You will have found reasons—excellent ones, for that matter—to refuse to make it.
[SCENE VI]
THE SAME, OSMONDE
(Osmonde enters briskly, a letter in her hand.)
OSMONDE : Papa, it was without your knowledge, I hope, that this letter was sent.
CLAUDE : What letter?
OSMONDE : Read it. (She hands the letter to Claude.)
EDMÉE : That individual showed you my letter? He really is unbelievable.
OSMONDE, to her father : What do you say to these insinuations?
CLAUDE : Listen, my darling, even admitting that your mother carried prudence a bit too far...
OSMONDE : There is no question of prudence. What is this way of protecting me like an object?
CLAUDE : Come now, there is nothing hurtful in that; it is quite natural that at your age one does not perceive certain dangers.
OSMONDE : What dangers? I ask that we finally dot the i's.
CLAUDE : The father of those little girls...
OSMONDE : You are afraid he takes pleasure in seeing me? Well! Yes, naturally, he didn't hide it from me. Besides, he is a widower.
CLAUDE : Osmonde, his wife is living.
OSMONDE : He is a widower, and if people push me to extremes...
EDMÉE : Is that a threat?
CLAUDE, in an undertone to Edmée : Leave me alone with her for a moment.
OSMONDE : Papa, tell her she has done a wicked thing.
EDMÉE : I hardly see the use of these conversations, but if it gives you pleasure...
OSMONDE : Mother is right, it serves no purpose. (Claude has approached her and tenderly placed his hand on her shoulder; Edmée looks at her with a spiteful smile and exits.)
[SCENE VII]
CLAUDE : My darling, you are on a dangerous slope.
OSMONDE : That word again!...
CLAUDE : I have just now understood what your reticence meant the other day.
